slides.text: Most people sort both words and compare. That's O(n log n).
slides.alt: Two racks of word-game tiles, both sorted to E I L N S T, above a code card: sorted("listen") == sorted("silent"), then "eilnst" == "eilnst" with an O(n log n) tag.

slides.text: +1 for every tile in the first rack, −1 for every tile in the second.
slides.alt: Racks spelling LISTEN and SILENT above a tally sheet with one row per letter, L, I, S, T, E and N; after the first rack every row reads +1.

slides.text: Every row back at zero means the same tiles.
slides.alt: The same tally sheet with all six rows back at 0, each ticked, and an ANAGRAM stamp.

slides.text: +1 for each letter of s, −1 for each letter of t; then every count must be 0.
slides.alt: Python function is_anagram(s, t) with the second loop, for ch in t: counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) - 1, highlighted. Under it the counts map for listen and silent with every letter at 0, and the note t: 't' → counts['t'] = 0.

slides.text: Our test run on 1,000,000 letters (Python): sorted() 215 ms, Counter 55 ms.
slides.alt: A stopwatch over two bars for 1,000,000 letters in our Python test run: sorted(s) == sorted(t) at 215 ms and Counter(s) == Counter(t) at 55 ms, with the label "counting: about ¼ of the time".

slides.text: Give it "café" and Python raises IndexError: list index out of range, while JavaScript quietly returns false.
slides.alt: "The catch: a 26-slot array covers a to z only" over a strip of slots a to z. Tiles C A F É point to "slot 136?"; Python crashes with IndexError: list index out of range, and JavaScript returns false, quietly wrong.
